item.question_text: A model-training platform is reached through a single login, "ds-admin", that four data engineers share and that carries administrative rights. One of those engineers moved to the finance department six weeks ago; his own named account on the platform is still enabled, although he no longer works with the platform. Applying identity-lifecycle reasoning, which course of action best fits the arrangement?

options.text: Retain the shared login only where an operational need for it has been specifically approved and recorded, and disable the mover's named account promptly.
Keep the shared login unchanged provided its password is rotated after each maintenance session, and leave the mover's account until the annual access review.
Issue each engineer a second platform identity alongside the shared one, and keep the mover's account live so his earlier reports stay reachable.
Reclassify the shared login as a service identity so that no approval is needed for it, and hand the mover's account over to his new finance manager.

item.explanation: Clause 5.16 of ISO/IEC 27002 allows shared identities only in limited circumstances: "identities assigned to multiple persons (e.g. shared identities) are only permitted where they are necessary for business or operational reasons and are subject to dedicated approval and documentation". The same guidance expects identities no longer required, including where the linked person has changed role, to be disabled or removed in a timely fashion, so the mover's account should not be left enabled.
item.key_support: identities assigned to multiple persons (e.g. shared identities) are only permitted where they are necessary for business or operational reasons and are subject to dedicated approval and documentation

distractor_support.support: identities are disabled or removed in a timely fashion if they are no longer required (e.g. if their associated entities are deleted or no longer used, or if the person linked to an identity has left the organization or changed the role)
distractor_support.why_wrong: Deferring removal to an annual review leaves an identity enabled after the linked person changed role, and password rotation does not substitute for the approval and documentation expected of a shared identity.

distractor_support.support: in a specific domain, a single identity is mapped to a single entity, [i.e. mapping of multiple identities to the same entity within the same context (duplicate identities) is avoided]
distractor_support.why_wrong: Adding named identities on top of the retained shared login creates duplicate identities for the same persons in one context, and retaining the mover's account for convenience ignores timely disabling.

distractor_support.support: identities assigned to non-human entities are subject to appropriately segregated approval and independent ongoing oversight
distractor_support.why_wrong: Labelling the login as non-human does not remove the need for approval and oversight, and passing a person's identity to another manager breaks the link between one identity and one accountable person.

item.question_text: A bank runs a retrieval-augmented assistant. Its parts are: a fine-tuned model weights file, a vector store holding embeddings of customer correspondence, a log of prompts and generated replies, and the GPU cluster hosting the service. The project team has listed the parts in a spreadsheet but left the accountability column empty, arguing the weights and embeddings are machine artefacts rather than records. Applying the Annex A control on inventories of information and other associated assets, what should the team do?

options.text: Record the weights file, vector store, prompt log and cluster as assets, and name for each entry the individual or group accountable for it.
Record only the GPU cluster and other tangible equipment, treating the weights and embeddings as derived outputs rather than assets.
Merge the four entries into one consolidated master list, since an inventory is only maintained when it is held as a single register.
Create a separate inventory entry for each short-lived inference container the service spawns while answering a user request.

item.explanation: Clause A.5.9 states that “An inventory of information and other associated assets, including owners, shall be developed and maintained.” The AI components hold or expose organizational information (customer correspondence embeddings, prompt and reply content, the tuned model and its hosting platform), so they belong in the inventory, and the entries are incomplete until accountability for each is recorded.
item.key_support: An inventory of information and other associated assets, including owners, shall be developed and maintained.

distractor_support.support: Information can be stored in many forms, including: digital form (e.g. data files stored on electronic or optical media), material form (e.g. on paper), as well as unrepresented information in the form of knowledge of the employees.
distractor_support.why_wrong: Digitally stored data such as embeddings of customer correspondence and tuned weights is information held in digital form, so it is not excluded from the inventory in favour of hardware alone.

distractor_support.support: The inventory does not need to be a single list of information and other associated assets.
distractor_support.why_wrong: A set of dynamic inventories maintained by the relevant functions is acceptable, so consolidation into one register is not what makes the inventory adequate.

distractor_support.support: Sometimes specific instances of assets in the information life cycle are not feasible to be documented due to the nature of the asset.
distractor_support.why_wrong: Granularity should suit the organization's needs, and short-lived instances such as transient compute instances are recognized as not always feasible to document individually.

item.question_text: A logistics firm keeps its customer contract database on a server where the administrator accounts still carry the vendor's default passwords. An organised crime group routinely scans the internet for such servers, copies the data it finds and resells it. Working from the ISO/IEC 27000 vocabulary, which element of this situation should be recorded as the threat?

options.text: The default passwords still in place on the server's administrator accounts
The organised crime group that scans for such servers and resells the data
The customer contract database that the firm holds on the server
The loss of confidentiality the firm would suffer if the data were resold

item.explanation: Clause 3.74 defines a threat as a "potential cause of an unwanted incident, which can result in harm to a system or organization", which in this scenario is the crime group acting against the firm. The default passwords are a weakness that the group could exploit, the database is the asset at risk, and the loss of confidentiality is the consequence, not the cause.
item.key_support: threat potential cause of an unwanted incident, which can result in harm to a system or organization (3.50)

distractor_support.support: vulnerability weakness of an asset or control (3.14) that can be exploited by one or more threats (3.74)
distractor_support.why_wrong: Unchanged default passwords are a weakness open to exploitation, so they are the vulnerability rather than the threat.

distractor_support.support: b) recognize that information, and related processes, systems, networks and people are important assets for achieving organization objectives;
distractor_support.why_wrong: The database is the information asset being protected, not the potential cause of the unwanted incident.

distractor_support.support: Note 4 to entry: Risk is often expressed in terms of a combination of the consequences of an event (including changes in circumstances) and the associated “likelihood” (as defined in ISO Guide 73:2009, 3.6.1.1) of occurrence.
distractor_support.why_wrong: Loss of confidentiality is the consequence that would follow the event, which is a separate element from the threat causing it.

item.question_text: An ISMS team is drafting the thresholds that will decide which analysed risks can be accepted without further action. One member proposes that the thresholds reflect the organization's objectives together with its internal and external circumstances, and that two of the impact levels be taken from a sector regulation the organization must observe. Which assessment of this proposal is best supported?

options.text: Basing the thresholds on organizational objectives and on internal and external circumstances is sound, and levels taken from regulation fit that basis.
Thresholds are properly derived from the levels of risk computed during the analysis step for each identified risk.
Thresholds are fixed after a treatment decision has been reached for each of the identified risks.
Management appetite alone furnishes the thresholds, with external standards and legal duties excluded from them.

item.explanation: Clause 3.66 states that risk criteria "are based on organizational objectives, and external context (3.22) and internal context (3.38)", and its second note adds that such criteria may come from standards, laws, policies and other requirements, so a threshold drawn from a sector regulation is consistent with that basis.
item.key_support: Note 1 to entry: Risk criteria are based on organizational objectives, and external context (3.22) and internal context (3.38).

distractor_support.support: risk evaluation process (3.54) of comparing the results of risk analysis (3.63) with risk criteria (3.66) to determine whether the risk (3.61) and/or its magnitude is acceptable or tolerable
distractor_support.why_wrong: Criteria are an independent term of reference that analysis results are compared against, not something derived from those results.

distractor_support.support: Before considering the treatment of a risk, the organization should define criteria for determining whether or not risks can be accepted.
distractor_support.why_wrong: The acceptance criteria are settled ahead of treatment decisions, not fixed afterwards.

distractor_support.support: Note 2 to entry: Risk criteria can be derived from standards, laws, policies (3.53) and other requirements (3.56).
distractor_support.why_wrong: Standards, laws and other requirements are recognised sources for risk criteria rather than excluded ones.
